You judge a requirements contract. A model interviewed the future users of a service and derived a contract from what they told it. You compare that contract with the reference requirements of the same service.

=== REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS (read-only) ===
BR-01: The service serves several independent operating companies at once. The staff of one operating company can never see or change another operating company's drones, models, sites, charging pads, jobs or flights, or their history.

BR-02: The airspace picture (the corridors between sites, the zones that group them, the prohibited zones and the closures) is one and the same for every company, and every company's staff can see all of it.

BR-03: Every member of staff acts in one of three roles: fleet technician or dispatcher at an operating company, or the airspace desk at the platform company. Each action of the service can be taken only by the role these requirements give it to.

BR-04: The airspace desk cannot see any one company's drones, jobs or flights.

BR-05: A fleet technician can add a drone to their company's fleet, stating its model. For each model the service holds how much it can carry, how far it can fly on a full battery, which sensors it carries, and which charging connector it uses.

BR-06: Each drone has a home site, one of its company's sites.

BR-07: A fleet technician can retire a drone. A retired drone stays in its company's history and is never again given a flight or sent to charge.

BR-08: A fleet technician can take a drone out of service for repair and put it back into service. A drone out of service cannot be given a flight.

BR-09: A fleet technician can set up a charging pad at one of their company's sites, stating its connector type.

BR-10: A charging pad is used only by drones of the company that owns it.

BR-11: A fleet technician can send a drone to charge. The service sends it only to a pad whose connector type is the one the drone's model uses, and refuses otherwise.

BR-12: The service keeps, for each drone, a record of when it was taken out of service, repaired or serviced, and put back, and by whom, so that its company can show a regulator how the drone has been looked after.

BR-13: A dispatcher can record a delivery job: a load to be carried from one site to another.

BR-14: A dispatcher can record an inspection job: the sensors it needs and a list of points to visit in a set order, ending back where it started.

BR-15: A dispatcher plans a flight for a job by choosing the drone and the way, a chain of corridors between named sites.

BR-16: The service never chooses a drone or a way for a flight, and never puts one in place of the dispatcher's choice.

BR-17: On a dispatcher's request, the service shows which of their company's drones could get to where a job starts.

BR-18: A flight leaves only after a dispatcher has signed it off; nothing but a dispatcher's own action signs a flight off.

BR-19: A dispatcher can call off a flight.

BR-20: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose drone cannot do the job: a load heavier than its model can carry, a way longer than its model can fly, or, for an inspection, a sensor the job needs that its model does not carry.

BR-21: The service refuses to sign off a flight whose way passes through a zone where flying is prohibited, or through a closure in force at any time during the flight.

BR-22: The service does not let more drones take off or land at a site at the same time than the site has places for.

BR-23: When dispatchers planning at the same time sign off flights that would use the same drone at overlapping times, only one sign-off succeeds, and the others are told why they failed.

BR-24: When it judges whether a drone can fly a way, the service does not count on the full range of a full battery, since batteries drain faster in cold and wind than planned.

BR-25: The service accepts reports from people and devices outside the company that a flight's load is ready, that its drone has reached a point of its job, and that it has arrived, and it records each against the flight.

BR-26: A report that arrives more than once is applied once.

BR-27: A report that arrives late or out of order never undoes a later one: a flight's state follows the order in which things happened, not the order in which the reports arrived.

BR-28: When a report a flight is waiting for does not come in time, such as its arrival, the service flags the flight to the dispatchers of its company, since nobody watches every drone.

BR-29: A drone that restarts in flight and carries on stays on the same flight, and its reports after the restart count for that flight.

BR-30: The airspace desk can record the corridors between named sites, the zones that group them, and the zones where the authorities prohibit flying.

BR-31: The airspace desk can enter a planned closure, with a start and an end time, and a sudden closure, which applies at once. It can amend a closure, for example by widening its area or moving its end time, and the amendment applies from the moment it is entered.

BR-32: When a closure is entered or amended, the service tells each company's dispatchers which of their flights it affects, including flights already in the air, and tells no company about another's flights.

BR-33: The service does not itself call off, reroute or change a flight because of a closure; that is the dispatcher's decision.

BR-34: When a closure is entered, the airspace desk sees how much disruption it caused across the customers, as totals that name no company and show no company's flights.

BR-35: The service can be restarted, or crash, while drones are flying, and afterwards carries on from where it was: nothing it had recorded is lost or applied twice.

BR-36: An instruction the service sends to a drone or to charging equipment takes effect once, even when it gets through twice or the service sends it again because it cannot tell whether the first attempt arrived.

BR-37: The service tells each company's own systems what happens to that company's drones and jobs, and nothing about any other company's.

BR-38: The service offers no way to steer a drone.
=== END OF REFERENCE REQUIREMENTS ===

The names in the reference that look like `name` stand for these values:
(none)

=== OUT OF SCOPE: things the users said they do not want ===
- Management or analytical reports, exports, and dashboards.
- Login through an external identity provider.
- i18n.
- Compliance with any regulation, or a compliance audit. Regulations are cited as provenance only (`domain-profile.md` §9).
- Data retention and erasure: no retention schedule, deletion on request, or pseudonymisation of history.
- Backups.
- High availability or multi-node deployment.
- User accounts, sign-up, passwords, or user management. Staff identities are issued outside the system; each request carries a signed token (D-23).
- Notifying people by e-mail, text message, or phone. Domain events go only to the event webhook (D-18).
- Route planning or automatic choice of a drone. The system validates the dispatcher's choice and never makes it (D-33).
- Remote piloting or real-time flight control. Flight control is on the drone (`domain-profile.md` §2).
- Weather data or forecasts.
- Billing, invoicing, or pricing of deliveries and inspections.
- Onboarding of new operating companies or management of tenants through the system.
=== TECHNICAL ADDITIONS: never stated by the users, and not counted against a contract ===
- Autoscaling.
- A second-level cache.
- A message broker, queue, or coordinator. Every boundary is HTTP (`domain-profile.md` §3).
- Geometric or geospatial computation. Position is a location or a corridor; coordinates, if present, are descriptive (`domain-profile.md` §4, §6).
- Throughput or latency at the declared scale. Scale is data context (`domain-profile.md` §7); the harness does not apply fleet-scale load during functional gates.
=== END OF LISTS ===

You receive the contract: a list of items, each with an id and a requirement.

For each reference requirement, decide how the contract as a whole covers it:

- covered: the items, together, state every obligation of the requirement — every rule, condition, exception, value and outcome it gives. Wording, order, the words chosen for states and roles, and whether a value is given by its name or by its number do not matter; meaning does.
- partial: the items state at least one of its obligations and leave out at least one other.
- missing: no item states any of its obligations.

An item states an obligation only when it says what the service must do, or must not do, in a case the requirement covers. A general wish, such as that the service be reliable, states none. An item that says the opposite of an obligation does not state it. A requirement that only names another one, or a value another one defines, does not take over that other requirement's obligations.

For each item of the contract, decide its class:

- reference: it states one or more obligations of the reference requirements; name each requirement it states obligations of.
- user_visible: it asks for something on the out-of-scope list.
- technical: it asks for something on the list of technical additions.
- other: none of these — it asks for something no reference requirement asks for, or states nothing checkable.

A contract with no items covers nothing.

Reply with JSON only: an object with two keys. "requirements" is a list with exactly one entry for every reference requirement, in the reference's order; each entry has "id", the requirement's id, "coverage", one of "covered", "partial" or "missing", and "items", the ids of the items that state its obligations (an empty list when it is missing). "items" is a list with exactly one entry for every item of the contract, in the contract's order; each entry has "id", the item's id, "class", one of "reference", "user_visible", "technical" or "other", and "requirements", the ids of the reference requirements it states obligations of (an empty list unless its class is "reference").

The contract has 132 items:

- id: DR-01
  requirement: The service must isolate each operating company's data so that users of one company cannot view or modify another company's drones, equipment, charging pads, sites, jobs, routes, customers, flight tracks, clearances, incidents, or maintenance records.
- id: DR-02
  requirement: When a new operating company is onboarded to the platform, the service must automatically give that company access to all active shared airspace zones, weather warnings, and platform airspace rules while keeping its operational data isolated from all other companies.
- id: DR-03
  requirement: The service must enforce role-based permissions for fleet technicians, dispatchers, and airspace desk users so that each user can perform only the actions assigned to their role.
- id: DR-04
  requirement: The service must prevent dispatchers and airspace desk users from creating or editing maintenance records, clearing maintenance or inspection holds, overriding overdue servicing or airworthiness blocks, or changing charging pad operational statuses.
- id: DR-05
  requirement: The service must prevent fleet technicians from creating customer jobs, dispatching flights, or approving airspace clearances.
- id: DR-06
  requirement: When presenting a flight plan or active flight to the airspace desk for clearance or monitoring, the service must display only the planned path or waypoints, altitude band, time window, drone model or performance category, an opaque flight and company reference, and a dispatcher contact channel.
- id: DR-07
  requirement: The service must hide customer names, cargo or payload descriptions, job descriptions, pricing, and internal maintenance records from the airspace desk.
- id: DR-08
  requirement: The service must record an immutable audit entry containing the timestamp and acting user for every change to drone status, equipment status, charging pad status, maintenance and inspection records, jobs, routes, clearances, overrides, incidents, and airspace zones.
- id: DR-09
  requirement: The service must store all timestamps unambiguously in UTC and display flight, job, and airspace restriction times in both UTC and the relevant local site time.
- id: DR-10
  requirement: The service must allow fleet technicians to register a new drone for their company with a unique identifier or registration number, model or type, home site, maximum payload weight, compatible payload or equipment types, maximum range or flight time, weather tolerances such as wind and rain limits, airworthiness certificate expiry date, and routine servicing intervals.
- id: DR-11
  requirement: When a new drone is registered, the service must place it in an initial maintenance or inspection status and prevent it from being assigned to flights or launched until a fleet technician clears it as ready.
- id: DR-12
  requirement: The service must track each drone's current operational status as one of maintenance or inspection, ready, flying, charging, or retired.
- id: DR-13
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to retire a drone only when it is not currently in flight and not assigned to any upcoming scheduled job.
- id: DR-14
  requirement: Once a drone is marked retired, the service must prevent it from returning to active service while retaining all of its historical flight, maintenance, and inspection records.
- id: DR-15
  requirement: The service must prevent a fleet technician from taking a drone out of service for maintenance while that drone is currently in flight.
- id: DR-16
  requirement: When a fleet technician takes a drone out of service for maintenance while it is assigned to upcoming scheduled jobs, the service must remove the drone from availability and alert dispatchers so those jobs can be reassigned.
- id: DR-17
  requirement: The service must allow fleet technicians to register swappable payload equipment modules, such as cold boxes, camera rigs, or sensor pods, with an identifier, equipment type, working status, calibration status or expiry date, and current drone attachment.
- id: DR-18
  requirement: The service must allow fleet technicians to attach and detach swappable payload equipment modules to and from drones in their company's fleet.
- id: DR-19
  requirement: The service must allow fleet technicians to configure charging pads at their company's sites with a pad identifier, site, compatible drone models or connector types, and status as available, occupied, or out of order.
- id: DR-20
  requirement: The service must allow a fleet technician to send a drone to charge on a pad only if the drone is currently at that site, is not flying or retired, and the selected pad is available and compatible with that drone.
- id: DR-21
  requirement: While a drone is charging on a pad, the service must mark the drone as charging and the pad as occupied, and update the drone's battery percentage as it charges up to 100 percent.
- id: DR-22
  requirement: When charging finishes or a technician unplugs a drone without active faults or holds, the service must return the pad status to available and the drone status to ready.
- id: DR-23
  requirement: When a fleet technician marks a charging pad as out of order, the service must prevent drones from being sent or reserved to charge on it and alert the technician if a drone is currently charging on that pad.
- id: DR-24
  requirement: When a flight is scheduled to land at a site equipped with charging pads, the service must support checking and reserving compatible pad capacity for the planned arrival window, while allowing ground staff to override pad reservations during an emergency landing.
- id: DR-25
  requirement: When a flight completes, the service must automatically update the drone's remaining battery percentage, cumulative flight hours, and flight cycles from flight telemetry, and allow a fleet technician to record battery checks manually when telemetry is unavailable.
- id: DR-26
  requirement: The service must allow fleet technicians to record repair and servicing logs specifying the drone, date and time, performing technician, work carried out, parts replaced, and inspection pass or fail sign-off.
- id: DR-27
  requirement: The service must track routine servicing intervals by flight hours, flight cycles, and calendar days, and alert fleet technicians when a drone is due or overdue for servicing.
- id: DR-28
  requirement: The service must block a drone from being dispatched or cleared to fly if it is in maintenance or inspection, is overdue for routine servicing, has an expired airworthiness certificate, has an open critical fault, or carries required equipment that is faulty or out of calibration.
- id: DR-29
  requirement: If a drone reports an in-flight mechanical fault, experiences a hard landing, or has an incident flagged by a dispatcher upon landing, the service must automatically place the drone into maintenance or inspection status and alert fleet technicians.
- id: DR-30
  requirement: The service must allow fleet technicians to generate a regulatory compliance report for any company drone over a chosen period showing all maintenance logs, inspection sign-offs, flight history, and verification that the drone did not fly while out of service, overdue, or unairworthy.
- id: DR-31
  requirement: The service must allow dispatchers to manage sites for their company, recording each site's name, geographic coordinates or address, site type, optional operating hours, sole-company ownership indicator, and ground or charging capacity.
- id: DR-32
  requirement: The service must allow dispatchers to create jobs containing a customer or client reference, job type, priority level, origin and destination sites or inspection waypoints, payload weight, required equipment or capabilities, and requested time window or deadline.
- id: DR-33
  requirement: The service must allow dispatchers to define flight routes connecting origin, intermediate waypoints or survey paths, and destination or return base, including planned altitude band, distance, and estimated flight time.
- id: DR-34
  requirement: Where a delivery job requires the drone to return to a base after drop-off, the service must include the return leg in the planned route, schedule, and battery budget.
- id: DR-35
  requirement: The service must allow dispatchers to configure recurring route templates with a route, schedule frequency or days of the week, time of day, and required drone specifications, and automatically generate scheduled jobs from active templates unless paused or cancelled.
- id: DR-36
  requirement: When matching or assigning a drone to a job, the service must verify that the drone belongs to the same company, is ready or scheduled to be ready at the origin site in time, meets payload weight and equipment requirements, and satisfies maintenance, airworthiness, and calibration rules.
- id: DR-37
  requirement: When matching or scheduling a flight, the service must verify that the drone's battery level and range are sufficient for the full planned route plus the configured safety reserve, and that forecast weather at the sites and along the route is within the drone's tolerances.
- id: DR-38
  requirement: The service must prevent two jobs from double-booking the same drone for overlapping time windows, including when multiple dispatchers edit the schedule concurrently.
- id: DR-39
  requirement: Unless a flight is an emergency diversion, the service must prevent scheduling a takeoff or landing at a site outside that site's configured operating hours and prevent exceeding the site's configured drone capacity.
- id: DR-40
  requirement: The service must track each job through its lifecycle statuses of draft or planned, scheduled, pending airspace clearance, cleared, in flight, and completed, as well as cancelled, failed, or aborted.
- id: DR-41
  requirement: The service must highlight high-priority jobs such as urgent medical transfers at the top of dispatchers' queues and allow dispatchers to reassign drones from lower-priority scheduled jobs when necessary.
- id: DR-42
  requirement: When a scheduled job is cancelled before takeoff, the service must immediately release the assigned drone and any reserved charging pad slot so they become available for other jobs.
- id: DR-43
  requirement: Immediately before a flight is launched, the service must confirm that the drone is ready, not overdue for service or unairworthy, has required working equipment, has sufficient battery with safety reserve, has valid airspace clearance if required, and has site and route weather within the drone's limits, blocking launch if any check fails.
- id: DR-44
  requirement: While a flight is active, the service must display to the company's dispatchers the drone's live position, altitude, speed, heading, battery level, route progress, live weather, and any relevant airspace alerts.
- id: DR-45
  requirement: If an active drone stops sending telemetry beyond a configured timeout, the service must raise a lost-link alert to the dispatcher, display the drone's last known position and timestamp, and allow the dispatcher to record manual status updates or mark the drone lost or recovered.
- id: DR-46
  requirement: During an active flight, the service must allow the dispatcher to issue hold or hover, return-to-base, or diversion commands to an alternate or emergency landing site and record the reason as an incident.
- id: DR-47
  requirement: If a drone lands at a location other than its originally planned destination, the service must update the drone's current location to the actual landing site.
- id: DR-48
  requirement: The service must provide a shift handover view for dispatchers showing all active flights, open alerts, pending clearances, priority jobs, timestamps, and dispatcher notes.
- id: DR-49
  requirement: The service must provide dispatchers with operational summaries of completed, delayed, and failed jobs as well as downloadable flight logs for their company's clients.
- id: DR-50
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to create, update, and deactivate shared airspace zones including permanent no-fly zones, temporary flight restrictions, special-permit or controlled zones, and weather warnings or advisories.
- id: DR-51
  requirement: For each airspace zone or weather warning, the service must store a polygon or circle geometry, minimum and maximum altitudes, effective start and end times or permanent flag, restriction type, severity or rule, and authority reference.
- id: DR-52
  requirement: When an airspace zone or weather warning expires or is deactivated, the service must retain it in historical records for regulatory audits rather than deleting it.
- id: DR-53
  requirement: Where multiple airspace zones overlap in geography, altitude, and time, the service must apply the strictest applicable restriction rule to any intersecting route.
- id: DR-54
  requirement: When the airspace desk creates or updates a restriction zone or weather warning, the service must immediately apply it across all companies, invalidate affected clearances or flag affected planned jobs, alert affected dispatchers, and send urgent alerts to both dispatchers and the airspace desk for any active flights inside or approaching the affected area.
- id: DR-55
  requirement: The service must automatically block any planned route or launch that intersects an active permanent no-fly zone, an active temporary flight restriction without an authorized waiver, or a severe weather warning.
- id: DR-56
  requirement: The service must place a scheduled flight into pending clearance and require manual approval from the airspace desk whenever its route enters a controlled or special-permit zone, exceeds standard altitude ceilings or visual-line-of-sight rules, requests an emergency or restriction waiver, or conflicts with another company's scheduled flight.
- id: DR-57
  requirement: The service must check all scheduled flights against one another for spatial and temporal overlap using configured horizontal and vertical separation minimums.
- id: DR-58
  requirement: When two scheduled flights of the same company violate separation minimums, the service must warn that company's dispatchers directly during planning.
- id: DR-59
  requirement: When two scheduled flights of different companies violate separation minimums, the service must alert the airspace desk and each affected company's dispatchers without disclosing the other company's identity or commercial details.
- id: DR-60
  requirement: The service must place high-priority clearance requests, such as urgent medical flights, at the top of the airspace desk's review queue and allow the desk to record an official waiver reference when approving flights under authorized emergency exceptions.
- id: DR-61
  requirement: When reviewing a clearance request, the service must allow the airspace desk to approve it with optional conditions such as altitude caps or corridor limits, request modifications, or reject it with a reason that returns the job to planning.
- id: DR-62
  requirement: If a dispatcher modifies a cleared flight's route, altitude, or scheduled time window beyond approved tolerances, or if a newly added restriction or flight conflict affects it, the service must automatically invalidate the existing clearance and require re-approval before takeoff.
- id: DR-63
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to issue standing clearances for approved recurring routes within defined parameters, and automatically revoke or flag them for re-review if intersecting airspace rules change.
- id: DR-64
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to configure platform-wide default horizontal and vertical separation minimums, standard altitude ceilings, and alert lead times.
- id: DR-65
  requirement: When urgent airspace or conflict alerts are sent for active or imminent flights, the service must record whether and when each responsible dispatcher and airspace desk user acknowledged the alert.
- id: DR-66
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to generate a platform-wide airspace compliance report over a chosen period detailing cleared flights, standing permits, emergency waivers, airspace infringements, and issued alerts. ```

  requirement: Unless a flight is an emergency diversion, the service must prevent scheduling a takeoff or landing at a site outside that site's configured operating hours and prevent exceeding the site's configured drone capacity.
- id: DR-106
  requirement: The service must track each job through its lifecycle statuses of draft or planned, scheduled, pending airspace clearance, cleared, in flight, and completed, as well as cancelled, failed, or aborted.
- id: DR-107
  requirement: The service must highlight high-priority jobs such as urgent medical transfers at the top of dispatchers' queues and allow dispatchers to reassign drones from lower-priority scheduled jobs when necessary.
- id: DR-108
  requirement: When a scheduled job is cancelled before takeoff, the service must immediately release the assigned drone and any reserved charging pad slot so they become available for other jobs.
- id: DR-109
  requirement: Immediately before a flight is launched, the service must confirm that the drone is ready, not overdue for service or unairworthy, has required working equipment, has sufficient battery with safety reserve, has valid airspace clearance if required, and has site and route weather within the drone's limits, blocking launch if any check fails.
- id: DR-110
  requirement: While a flight is active, the service must display to the company's dispatchers the drone's live position, altitude, speed, heading, battery level, route progress, live weather, and any relevant airspace alerts.
- id: DR-111
  requirement: If an active drone stops sending telemetry beyond a configured timeout, the service must raise a lost-link alert to the dispatcher, display the drone's last known position and timestamp, and allow the dispatcher to record manual status updates or mark the drone lost or recovered.
- id: DR-112
  requirement: During an active flight, the service must allow the dispatcher to issue hold or hover, return-to-base, or diversion commands to an alternate or emergency landing site and record the reason as an incident.
- id: DR-113
  requirement: If a drone lands at a location other than its originally planned destination, the service must update the drone's current location to the actual landing site.
- id: DR-114
  requirement: The service must provide a shift handover view for dispatchers showing all active flights, open alerts, pending clearances, priority jobs, timestamps, and dispatcher notes.
- id: DR-115
  requirement: The service must provide dispatchers with operational summaries of completed, delayed, and failed jobs as well as downloadable flight logs for their company's clients.
- id: DR-116
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to create, update, and deactivate shared airspace zones including permanent no-fly zones, temporary flight restrictions, special-permit or controlled zones, and weather warnings or advisories.
- id: DR-117
  requirement: For each airspace zone or weather warning, the service must store a polygon or circle geometry, minimum and maximum altitudes, effective start and end times or permanent flag, restriction type, severity or rule, and authority reference.
- id: DR-118
  requirement: When an airspace zone or weather warning expires or is deactivated, the service must retain it in historical records for regulatory audits rather than deleting it.
- id: DR-119
  requirement: Where multiple airspace zones overlap in geography, altitude, and time, the service must apply the strictest applicable restriction rule to any intersecting route.
- id: DR-120
  requirement: When the airspace desk creates or updates a restriction zone or weather warning, the service must immediately apply it across all companies, invalidate affected clearances or flag affected planned jobs, alert affected dispatchers, and send urgent alerts to both dispatchers and the airspace desk for any active flights inside or approaching the affected area.
- id: DR-121
  requirement: The service must automatically block any planned route or launch that intersects an active permanent no-fly zone, an active temporary flight restriction without an authorized waiver, or a severe weather warning.
- id: DR-122
  requirement: The service must place a scheduled flight into pending clearance and require manual approval from the airspace desk whenever its route enters a controlled or special-permit zone, exceeds standard altitude ceilings or visual-line-of-sight rules, requests an emergency or restriction waiver, or conflicts with another company's scheduled flight.
- id: DR-123
  requirement: The service must check all scheduled flights against one another for spatial and temporal overlap using configured horizontal and vertical separation minimums.
- id: DR-124
  requirement: When two scheduled flights of the same company violate separation minimums, the service must warn that company's dispatchers directly during planning.
- id: DR-125
  requirement: When two scheduled flights of different companies violate separation minimums, the service must alert the airspace desk and each affected company's dispatchers without disclosing the other company's identity or commercial details.
- id: DR-126
  requirement: The service must place high-priority clearance requests, such as urgent medical flights, at the top of the airspace desk's review queue and allow the desk to record an official waiver reference when approving flights under authorized emergency exceptions.
- id: DR-127
  requirement: When reviewing a clearance request, the service must allow the airspace desk to approve it with optional conditions such as altitude caps or corridor limits, request modifications, or reject it with a reason that returns the job to planning.
- id: DR-128
  requirement: If a dispatcher modifies a cleared flight's route, altitude, or scheduled time window beyond approved tolerances, or if a newly added restriction or flight conflict affects it, the service must automatically invalidate the existing clearance and require re-approval before takeoff.
- id: DR-129
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to issue standing clearances for approved recurring routes within defined parameters, and automatically revoke or flag them for re-review if intersecting airspace rules change.
- id: DR-130
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to configure platform-wide default horizontal and vertical separation minimums, standard altitude ceilings, and alert lead times.
- id: DR-131
  requirement: When urgent airspace or conflict alerts are sent for active or imminent flights, the service must record whether and when each responsible dispatcher and airspace desk user acknowledged the alert.
- id: DR-132
  requirement: The service must allow the airspace desk to generate a platform-wide airspace compliance report over a chosen period detailing cleared flights, standing permits, emergency waivers, airspace infringements, and issued alerts.
